title: Postgres slow-query profiler CLI
subtitle: Three rounds across five territories. The .com collapse is the finding: move to .dev, or buy.
domain_mode: B — available on .com or a developer-native TLD

brief.does: Reads your Postgres slow-query log and tells you which index is missing
brief.audience: Backend engineers, typing it in a terminal several times a day
brief.positioning: Precision instrument, not a startup product. Sits against full observability platforms by doing one thing without an agent or a dashboard.
brief.personality: Technical, precise, unfashionable in a good way
brief.constraints: Short and typeable. One word under 8 characters preferred. npm and PyPI wanted free for future installers.

assumptions: Go binary distributed via a Homebrew tap
No commercial launch yet, so trademark and app stores are out of scope

territories.name: Depth sounding
territories.description: The instruments sailors used to find the bottom before sonar — a weighted line dropped into water you cannot see through.
territories.fit: The product's job is finding the expensive thing hidden in a system you have no visibility into. Maps almost exactly.

territories.name: Diagnostics
territories.description: Vitals, triage, symptoms, the patient chart.
territories.fit: Fits the function, but every observability tool already lives here, so expect to sound like the category.
territories.note: crowded by meaning, not by domain

territories.name: Divining
territories.description: Finding water underground by reading surface signals.
territories.fit: Generates well and the mechanism is right. Cuts against 'precision tooling' — see the Dowse weakness.

territories.name: Craft and sharpening
territories.description: Whetstone, hone, grindstone, the tools that make other tools work.
territories.fit: Fits 'make the slow thing fast', but heavily used across developer tooling already.

territories.name: Cartography of the plan tree
territories.description: Atlas, contour, seam — the query plan as terrain.
territories.fit: Accurate but abstract; the names read as generic data tooling.

rounds.focus: Spread across all five territories, .com and .dev
rounds.note: 1/24 on **.com**, 14/24 on **.dev**. Real-word compounds on .com were registered between 1995 and 2010. This decides the TLD, not the name.
Rate held. Same conclusion, more confidently.

rounds.focus: Strongest stems, short CLI-shaped forms, added .sh
rounds.note: Short single words are gone on .com and free on .dev and .sh.

candidates.name: Sounder
candidates.why: The instrument itself, and a real word an engineer reads correctly on first sight. Shortest of the finalists and the best as a typed command: `sounder analyze`.
candidates.weakness: Also a bird and an audio device, and it reads as a comparative adjective ("sounder judgment") on first pass. PyPI is taken, so a Python installer needs a different distribution name.

clearance.detail: checked the name alone, not name + postgres

candidates.name: Leadsman
candidates.why: The leadsman is the crew member who drops the weighted line and calls the depth. That is precisely this tool's role: not the navigator, the one who reports what is under you. Two syllables, spells itself, no collision in developer tooling.
candidates.weakness: The reference is invisible unless you know it, and non-nautical readers hear "lead" as sales lead first — an unfortunate association in a B2B-adjacent space.
candidates.verdict: Pick it if your audience enjoys a name that rewards knowing something.

candidates.name: Dowse
candidates.why: Five letters, one syllable, unclaimed on both developer TLDs. The metaphor is exactly right: finding what is underground by reading surface signals.
candidates.weakness: Dowsing is pseudoscience. For a tool selling itself on precision, naming it after the archetypal unscientific method is a real tension — some engineers will read it as a joke.
candidates.verdict: Best shape of the three. Only works if the association reads as confident rather than careless.

candidates.name: By the Mark
candidates.why: The leadsman's actual call — "by the mark, twain" — the depth read off the knots on the line. It names the output rather than the operator, which is the more accurate framing for a reporting tool.
candidates.weakness: Three words. As a CLI binary it has to collapse to `bythemark` or `btm`, and neither is good. Better suited to a hosted product than a terminal command.
candidates.verdict: Highest ceiling, wrong shape for a CLI.

candidates.name: Plumbline
candidates.why: The weight on a string that finds true vertical. Familiar to people who have never been on a boat, which removes the explanation cost that Leadsman carries.
candidates.weakness: Nine characters and two stressed syllables, so it types and speaks heavier than the rest. Both `.com` and `.dev` are registered, which leaves no clean domain route.
candidates.verdict: Better word, worse availability. Listed so you can see what was given up.

candidates.name: Slipstream
candidates.why: The low-drag pocket behind a moving object — the state the tool is trying to put your queries into. Instantly understood with no domain knowledge.
candidates.weakness: Heavily used as a product name across several industries, and it describes the outcome rather than the mechanism, which makes it interchangeable with any performance tool.
candidates.verdict: Aftermarket only, and not worth it at BrandBucket pricing.

candidates.name: Deadreckon
candidates.why: Dead reckoning is estimating position from known speed and heading when you cannot see landmarks — a fair description of query planning itself.
candidates.weakness: "Dead" in the name of a database tool is an unforced association with downtime. The `.dev` lookup did not resolve.
candidates.verdict: Weak on tone. Resolve the lookup before spending more thought on it.

domains.detail: HTTP 429 after 4 attempts — unresolved, not available

top3.name: Sounder
top3.reason: Types well, reads correctly cold, and the metaphor survives without explanation.
top3.dealbreaker: Drop it if the PyPI collision matters more than I think.

top3.name: Leadsman
top3.dealbreaker: Drop it if a meaningful share of your audience will hear "sales lead".

top3.name: Dowse
top3.reason: Best shape of all three and free on both developer TLDs.
top3.dealbreaker: Drop it if "precision tooling" is the positioning you have to defend.

unconventional.name: By the Mark
unconventional.reason: A phrase name in developer tooling is rare enough to be memorable.
unconventional.cost: You give up the clean binary name — it collapses to `bythemark` or `btm`.

unverified: Search was run on the names alone, not on "name + postgres". A same-category collision could still exist — check before you announce.
`deadreckon.dev` returned HTTP 429 after four attempts. That is **unresolved, not available**.
No trademark search. Correct for a hobby CLI, wrong the moment you charge for it.
GitHub `taken` results confirm the org exists, nothing more. Several are dormant accounts, which does not help — GitHub rarely releases them.
Social handles were not checked. Platform status codes are unreliable in both directions; open the signup pages yourself.
